# Results — Study 41 (Hangover): the January Barometer on the S&P 500, 1950–2025

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly total return of the **S&P 500
(^GSPC)**, daily from Yahoo resampled to month-end, 1950–2025 (**76 years**). The omen: sign(January)
predicts sign(rest-of-year). As-of **2026-06-30**; inputs fingerprint `ad00d963be48`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Predicts the year"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The January Barometer's *directional* claim — as goes January, so goes the year — is `NOT SUPPORTED`
against the only honest benchmark, the **base rate**. The rest of the year is up **76%** of the time
*unconditionally* (stocks just rise); the omen's directional accuracy is **68%** — it is **beaten by a
constant that always predicts "up"**. There is a `WEAK` real residue: a *down* January does precede a
softer rest-of-year (**+2.1%, up 60%** vs **+12.2%, up 87%** after an up January), so sitting in cash
after a down January cuts drawdown (−40% → −16%, Sharpe 0.57 → 0.69). But that's `MIRAGE` tradability:
the "timing" just **reduces equity exposure** — a permanently smaller stock weight does the same — it
acts once a year, and it has **decayed** since Yale Hirsch coined the omen in 1972.

## Data stamp

- **Index**: S&P 500 (^GSPC) monthly TR, 1950 → 2025, 76 years, inputs fingerprint `ad00d963be48`

## The omen vs the base rate

| | n | rest-of-year mean | P(rest-of-year up) |
|---|---|---|---|
| after an **up** January | 46 | **+12.2%** | 87% |
| after a **down** January | 30 | **+2.1%** | 60% |
| **unconditional** (the base rate) | 76 | +8.2% | **76%** |

> Directional accuracy of the omen: **68.4%** — *below* the 76.3% you get by always predicting "up".
> As a *predictor*, the barometer is worse than ignoring January entirely.

The believers' headline ("the rest of the year is up 87% after an up January!") is a **base-rate
illusion**: the rest of the year is up most of the time *regardless*. The only informative cell is the
down-January one — and even there the market still rises on average.

## The tradable version vs just holding the index

| (rest-of-year only) | CAGR | annual Sharpe | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buy & hold (Feb–Dec, every year) | **+7.2%** | 0.57 | −40% |
| Barometer (cash after a down January) | +6.9% | **0.69** | **−16%** |

The barometer gives up return for a higher Sharpe and a much shallower drawdown — but only because it
is **out of the market** in ~40% of down-January years. It isn't timing the market; it's holding less
of it. A static lower-equity weight buys the same risk reduction without the calendar story.

## Why it's weak, not real: post-publication decay

| | directional accuracy | down-January rest-of-year |
|---|---|---|
| 1950–1972 (before Hirsch named it) | **78%** | **−0.4%** |
| 1973–2025 (after) | 64% | **+3.0%** |

The omen was sharpest *before* it was famous (a down January genuinely preceded a flat-to-down year),
and faded once everyone watched it — the textbook McLean–Pontiff signature. What survives today is a
faint, decayed, exposure-reducing tic, not a forecast.

## The honest takeaway

The January Barometer is **not a forecaster** — as a directional omen it loses to "stocks go up". Its
one measurable residue (a down January precedes a weaker year) is real but small, has decayed since
publication, and "trades" only by cutting equity exposure once a year. `WEAK` signal, `MIRAGE`
tradability, `NOT SUPPORTED` as the year-ahead barometer it's sold as.
